sections.title: The Final Plague Announced
observations: In this section, God informs Moses about the final plague that will strike Egypt, which will lead to the liberation of the Israelites. This plague is significant as it represents the culmination of God's judgment against Pharaoh and the Egyptian gods.

God's declaration that every firstborn in Egypt will die emphasizes the severity of the judgment and the lengths to which God will go to free His people. It also serves as a direct challenge to the Egyptian belief in the power of their gods, particularly those associated with fertility and life.

sections.title: The Israelites' Favor in Egypt
observations: God instructs Moses that the Israelites will receive favor from the Egyptians, which is a remarkable turn of events considering the oppression they faced. This favor will result in the Israelites asking for and receiving silver and gold from their neighbors.

This act of giving is not just a means of compensation for the years of slavery but also serves a greater purpose in God's plan, as these materials will later be used in the construction of the Tabernacle.

sections.title: The Plague of the Firstborn
observations: The announcement of the plague is followed by a description of the devastation it will cause. The death of the firstborn is a profound loss that will resonate throughout Egypt, affecting every household.

This event is pivotal in the narrative of Exodus, as it leads to the final release of the Israelites from bondage. It also foreshadows the Passover, where the blood of a lamb will protect the Israelites from this judgment.

importantVerses.commentary: Moses declares that at midnight, the Lord will go through Egypt and strike down every firstborn. This verse highlights the seriousness of God's judgment and the specific timing of His actions.
God tells Moses that Pharaoh will not listen, which underscores the hardness of Pharaoh's heart and the futility of his resistance against God's will.

questions: What does the final plague reveal about God's sovereignty over nations and rulers?
How does the favor shown to the Israelites reflect God's provision and care for His people?
In what ways does the concept of the firstborn in this chapter connect to the New Testament understanding of Christ as the firstborn?
